source_refs.note: Exercise 1.4, Question 2: book p. 28, Q2 (i)-(vi) exponential and logarithmic inequalities; answer key book p. 299 (PDF 301)

blocks.prompt: 2 (i) Solve the inequality (if its solution exists): \(2^x + 2^{1-x} \le 3\).
blocks.explanation:
An exponential inequality with \(2^x\) and \(2^{1-x} = \frac{2}{2^x}\).
Plan: put \(y = 2^x > 0\), multiply by \(y\) (sign kept), solve the quadratic inequality, then go back to \(x\) (base 2 > 1, sign kept).
steps:
Given: \(2^x + 2^{1-x} \le 3\).
To find: all real \(x\) satisfying it.
Method: \(2^{1-x} = \frac{2}{2^x}\), so \(y = 2^x\) gives \(y + \frac{2}{y} \le 3\); since \(y > 0\), multiplying by \(y\) keeps the sign.

Domain
\[\text{Domain} = ]-\infty, \infty[\]
Why: exponentials are defined for every real number.

Substitute \(y = 2^x\) (\(y > 0\))
\[y + \dfrac{2}{y} \le 3\]
\[y^2 + 2 \le 3y\]
\[y^2 - 3y + 2 \le 0\]
\[(y - 1)(y - 2) \le 0\]
Why: \(y > 0\), so multiplying by \(y\) does not change the sign.

Solve for \(y\)
\[1 \le y \le 2\]
Why: a product of two factors is \(\le 0\) when \(y\) lies between the roots 1 and 2.

Back to \(x\)
\[2^0 \le 2^x \le 2^1\]
\[0 \le x \le 1\]
Why: base \(2 > 1\), so \(2^x\) is increasing and the signs are kept.

Check:
\(x = 0.5\): \(2^{0.5} + 2^{0.5} = 2\sqrt{2} \approx 2.83 \le 3\) \(\checkmark\)
\(x = 2\): \(4 + 0.5 = 4.5 > 3\), outside, as expected.
Ends: \(x = 0\) gives \(1 + 2 = 3\), \(x = 1\) gives \(2 + 1 = 3\), so both ends are included.

blocks.prompt: 2 (ii) Solve the inequality (if its solution exists): \(2^x \ge \log_2(16)\).
blocks.explanation:
The right side is just a number: \(\log_2 16 = 4\).
Plan: write 4 as a power of 2 and compare exponents (base 2 > 1, sign kept).
steps:
Given: \(2^x \ge \log_2(16)\).
To find: all real \(x\) satisfying it.
Method: simplify the right side, write it as a power of 2, then use that \(2^x\) is increasing.

Domain
\[\text{Domain} = ]-\infty, \infty[\]
Why: \(2^x\) is defined for every real number, and \(\log_2 16\) is a fixed number.

Simplify the right side
\[\log_2 16 = \log_2 2^4 = 4\]
\[2^x \ge 4 = 2^2\]
Why: \(\log_a a^k = k\).

Compare the exponents
\[x \ge 2\]
Why: base \(2 > 1\), so the exponential function is increasing and the sign is kept.

Check:
\(x = 3\): \(8 \ge 4\) \(\checkmark\)
\(x = 1\): \(2 \ge 4\) is false, as expected.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key prints \(S = [2, \infty]\). Since \(\infty\) is not a real number it can never be included, so the bracket at \(\infty\) must be open: \(S = [2, \infty[\).

blocks.prompt: 2 (iii) Solve the inequality (if its solution exists): \(\log_2(x - 1) \ge \log_2(5 - x)\).
blocks.explanation:
Both sides are logarithms to base 2.
Plan: find the domain, remove the logarithms (base 2 > 1, sign kept), solve the linear inequality and intersect with the domain.
steps:
Given: \(\log_2(x - 1) \ge \log_2(5 - x)\).
To find: all real \(x\) satisfying it.
Method: domain first; then \(\log_2\) is increasing, so the arguments keep the same order.

Domain
\[x - 1 > 0 \Rightarrow x > 1\]
\[5 - x > 0 \Rightarrow x < 5\]
\[\text{Domain} = ]1, 5[\]
Why: both logarithms need positive arguments.

Remove the logarithms
\[x - 1 \ge 5 - x\]
\[2x \ge 6\]
\[x \ge 3\]
Why: base \(2 > 1\), so the sign is kept.

Compatibility with the domain
\[3 \le x < 5\]
Why: \(x \ge 3\) together with \(1 < x < 5\). The end 5 is open because \(\log_2(5 - 5) = \log_2 0\) does not exist.

Check:
\(x = 4\): \(\log_2 3 \approx 1.585 \ge \log_2 1 = 0\) \(\checkmark\)
\(x = 2\): \(\log_2 1 = 0 \ge \log_2 3\) is false, as expected.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key prints \(S = [3, 5]\). The value \(x = 5\) makes \(\log_2(5 - x) = \log_2 0\), which is undefined, so 5 must be excluded: \(S = [3, 5[\).

blocks.prompt: 2 (iv) Solve the inequality (if its solution exists): \(\log_{\frac{1}{3}}(x^2 - 4x + 3) > \log_{\frac{1}{3}}(2x - 1)\).
blocks.explanation:
Both sides are logarithms to base \(\frac{1}{3}\), which is between 0 and 1.
Plan: find the domain, remove the logarithms with the sign reversed (decreasing function), solve the quadratic inequality, then intersect with each piece of the domain.
steps:
Given: \(\log_{\frac{1}{3}}(x^2 - 4x + 3) > \log_{\frac{1}{3}}(2x - 1)\).
To find: all real \(x\) satisfying it.
Method: domain first; since \(0 < \frac{1}{3} < 1\), \(\log_{\frac{1}{3}}\) is decreasing, so the bigger logarithm belongs to the smaller argument: the sign reverses.

Domain
\[x^2 - 4x + 3 = (x - 1)(x - 3) > 0\]
\[\Rightarrow x < 1 \text{ or } x > 3\]
\[2x - 1 > 0 \Rightarrow x > \tfrac{1}{2}\]
\[\text{Domain} = ]\tfrac{1}{2}, 1[ \cup ]3, \infty[\]
Why: both arguments must be positive at the same time.

Remove the logarithms (sign reversed)
\[x^2 - 4x + 3 < 2x - 1\]
\[x^2 - 6x + 4 < 0\]
Why: base \(\frac{1}{3}\) is between 0 and 1, so the function is decreasing.

Roots of \(x^2 - 6x + 4 = 0\)
\[x = \dfrac{6 \pm \sqrt{36 - 16}}{2}\]
\[= \dfrac{6 \pm 2\sqrt{5}}{2} = 3 \pm \sqrt{5}\]
Why: quadratic formula with \(a = 1,\ b = -6,\ c = 4\).

Where the quadratic is negative
\[3 - \sqrt{5} < x < 3 + \sqrt{5}\]
(about \(0.764 < x < 5.236\))
Why: an upward parabola is negative between its roots.

Compatibility with the domain
\[]\tfrac{1}{2}, 1[ \cap ]3 - \sqrt{5}, 3 + \sqrt{5}[\]
\[= ]3 - \sqrt{5}, 1[\]
\[]3, \infty[ \cap ]3 - \sqrt{5}, 3 + \sqrt{5}[\]
\[= ]3, 3 + \sqrt{5}[\]
Why: \(3 - \sqrt{5} \approx 0.764\) is bigger than \(\frac{1}{2}\), so the first piece starts at \(3 - \sqrt{5}\), not at \(\frac{1}{2}\).

Check with test points (\(L\) = left side, \(R\) = right side):
\(x = 0.6\): \(L \approx 0.037\), \(R \approx 1.465\): \(L > R\) false, so \(0.6\) is not a solution.
\(x = 0.9\): \(L \approx 1.421\), \(R \approx 0.203\): true.
\(x = 4\): \(L = -1\), \(R \approx -1.771\): true.
\(x = 6\): \(L \approx -2.465\), \(R \approx -2.183\): false.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key prints \(S = ]\frac{1}{2}, 1[ \cup ]3, 3 + \sqrt{5}[\). The first interval is wrong: the condition \(x^2 - 6x + 4 < 0\) must also hold there, which cuts it down to \(]3 - \sqrt{5}, 1[\). For example \(x = 0.6\) is in the key's interval, but \(\log_{\frac{1}{3}} 0.96 \approx 0.037\) is not greater than \(\log_{\frac{1}{3}} 0.2 \approx 1.465\). Correct: \(S = ]3 - \sqrt{5}, 1[ \cup ]3, 3 + \sqrt{5}[\).

blocks.prompt: 2 (v) Solve the inequality (if its solution exists): \(\log_2(x - 2) + \log_2(x - 3) \ge 3\).
blocks.explanation:
Two logarithms to base 2 on the left and a number on the right.
Plan: domain, product law, write 3 as \(\log_2 8\), remove the logarithm (sign kept), solve the quadratic inequality, intersect with the domain.
steps:
Given: \(\log_2(x - 2) + \log_2(x - 3) \ge 3\).
To find: all real \(x\) satisfying it.
Method: join the left side with the product law and write 3 as a logarithm to base 2, so both sides can be compared.

Domain
\[x - 2 > 0 \text{ and } x - 3 > 0\]
\[\text{Domain} = ]3, \infty[\]
Why: each logarithm in the original inequality needs a positive argument.

Product law and \(3 = \log_2 8\)
\[\log_2[(x - 2)(x - 3)] \ge \log_2 8\]
Why: \(\log_2 m + \log_2 n = \log_2(mn)\) and \(\log_2 2^3 = 3\).

Remove the logarithm
\[(x - 2)(x - 3) \ge 8\]
\[x^2 - 5x + 6 - 8 \ge 0\]
\[x^2 - 5x - 2 \ge 0\]
Why: base \(2 > 1\), so the sign is kept.

Roots of \(x^2 - 5x - 2 = 0\)
\[x = \dfrac{5 \pm \sqrt{25 + 8}}{2} = \dfrac{5 \pm \sqrt{33}}{2}\]
(about \(-0.372\) and \(5.372\))
The quadratic is \(\ge 0\) outside its roots:
\[x \le \dfrac{5 - \sqrt{33}}{2} \text{ or } x \ge \dfrac{5 + \sqrt{33}}{2}\]
Why: an upward parabola is non-negative outside its roots.

Compatibility with the domain
\(\frac{5 - \sqrt{33}}{2}\) is negative, so that part has no point with \(x > 3\). Only \(x \ge \frac{5 + \sqrt{33}}{2}\) remains (and \(5.372 > 3\)).
Why: the answer must also lie in \(]3, \infty[\).

Check:
\(x = 6\): \(\log_2 4 + \log_2 3 \approx 2 + 1.585 = 3.585 \ge 3\) \(\checkmark\)
\(x = 5\): \(\log_2 3 + \log_2 2 \approx 2.585 < 3\), outside, as expected.
At \(x = \frac{5 + \sqrt{33}}{2}\), \((x - 2)(x - 3) = 8\), so the left side is exactly 3 and the end point is included.

blocks.prompt: 2 (vi) Solve the inequality (if its solution exists): \(\log(x) + \log(x - 3) \ge \log(2x) + \log(x - 1)\).
blocks.explanation:
Two logarithms on each side, all to base 10. The question says "if its solution exists": here it does not.
Plan: domain, product law on both sides, remove the logarithms (sign kept), solve, intersect with the domain.
steps:
Given: \(\log(x) + \log(x - 3) \ge \log(2x) + \log(x - 1)\).
To find: all real \(x\) satisfying it, if any.
Method: join each side with the product law, then compare the arguments (base 10 is increasing).

Domain
\[x > 0,\ x > 3,\ x > 0,\ x > 1\]
\[\text{Domain} = ]3, \infty[\]
Why: all four arguments \(x,\ x - 3,\ 2x,\ x - 1\) must be positive; all four hold together only when \(x > 3\).

Product law on both sides
\[\log[x(x - 3)] \ge \log[2x(x - 1)]\]
Why: \(\log m + \log n = \log(mn)\).

Remove the logarithms
\[x^2 - 3x \ge 2x^2 - 2x\]
\[0 \ge x^2 + x\]
\[x(x + 1) \le 0\]
Why: base \(10 > 1\), so the sign is kept.

Solve
\[-1 \le x \le 0\]
Why: the product \(x(x + 1)\) is \(\le 0\) between its roots \(-1\) and \(0\).

Compatibility with the domain
No number satisfies both \(-1 \le x \le 0\) and \(x > 3\), so the inequality has no solution.

Check:
For any \(x > 3\): \(x < 2x\) and \(x - 3 < x - 1\), so \(x(x - 3) < 2x(x - 1)\): the left side is always smaller. For example \(x = 4\): \(\log 4 + \log 1 \approx 0.602\), while \(\log 8 + \log 3 \approx 1.380\).
